k: Designing how an AI behaves, not just how it looks

A B2B platform was putting an AI assistant at the centre of its product: one that could create, change and delete people’s work, and contact customers on their behalf. I defined how that assistant should behave and turned it into a design system the product and engineering teams could build from, in two months.
Audit, foundations, AI layer, documentation, handoff
Built by engineering, not yet live
The assistant could take real, sometimes irreversible actions, but the design system had no patterns for AI, weak foundations, and products drifting apart.
Stabilised the foundations, turned the product spec’s rules into a reusable AI layer of 45+ components, and documented it as rules the whole team could follow.
One shared definition of safe AI behaviour for design and engineering, now built by the engineering team.

k.i: Cover: an answer built from the AI components (steps, chart, access note, follow-ups)

k: The assistant was the product’s biggest bet. People could build workflows, update and delete work, and send e-signature requests just by typing a sentence. That speed is the value.

It’s also the risk. One misread request could delete a team’s work or contact a customer, and an e-signature request can’t be recalled once it’s sent. Whether people trusted the assistant would decide whether they used it, and that trust is won or lost in the interface.
Not missing components, a missing agreement
The gap wasn’t a few components. There was no shared answer to a basic question: what should the AI do before, during and after it acts?

Product had rules in a spec. Engineering needed parts they could build. Design had no AI patterns, so every feature would have invented its own version of “are you sure?”. Underneath that, the system itself wasn’t ready.
Nothing for showing the AI’s work, asking before acting, or admitting failure.
About 8 in 10 component colours were hard-coded. Names had typos and defaults like “Property 1”. Old UI-kit modals still used their own blue.
The workflow builder and run history used one-off elements, so the same thing looked different from screen to screen.

k.i: Before: the old form components, with inconsistent fonts, sizes and colours

k: Without a working system, each designer and engineer built screens from scratch. It worked at first, but the cost grew with every feature, and for an AI that acts on people’s work, inconsistency became a trust problem.
It didn’t feel like one product
About 8 in 10 component colours were hard-coded, old UI-kit buttons were still blue, and the workflow builder used one-off elements, so the same thing looked different from screen to screen.
Three tiers of tokens and cleaned-up components, so a change happens in one place.
The same work was done again and again
Designers redrew common parts, and engineers rebuilt the same components in slightly different ways, so effort went into repeating work instead of improving it.
Shared components with written rules, and a docs site engineers could build from directly.
Loading, empty, error and focus states had to be remembered screen by screen, and contrast and keyboard support were handled unevenly.
States and accessibility built into components, so getting them right once fixed them everywhere.
From the spec review and testing
Every AI feature invented its own safety

Confirmations, failure messages and AI labels differed from feature to feature, so people couldn’t form a habit. Testing later showed the risk: only 5 of 20 people checked the count before confirming a delete.
One trust model as components: confirmation tiers, honest failure notices and a distinct AI identity.
03  My role and how I led
I led the design of the AI layer from end to end. The product manager owned the spec and its rules; the engineering team built the system from my designs and documentation.
The system audit, the foundation fixes, every AI pattern and component, the guidelines and docs site, and the handoff to engineering.
How the spec’s risk rules became visible behaviour, worked through with the product manager, and how tokens and components mapped to code, worked through with engineering.
The product spec itself, the AI model and its prompts, or the build. Knowing where my work stopped kept decisions clear.
Making it the team’s system, not mine
A design system only works if people use it. So I spent as much effort on adoption as on the components themselves.
I ran walkthroughs of the system and reviewed new screens against it, so problems were caught in design, not in the build.
I worked alongside engineers as they used the components, answering questions and fixing gaps in the components and docs as they came up.
I set how others could add or change components, so the system could grow without drifting back into one-off parts.
I guided another designer on using the system and on designing for AI, so the knowledge didn’t sit with one person.
What I had to work within
Good constraints shaped the design as much as the brief did.
The system was in use while I changed it, so every fix had to keep existing screens working.
A separate AI design system would have split the team and slowed them down. The AI layer had to sit on the same tokens and components.
Confirmation had to happen inside the conversation, with no buttons; only three named tools could ever appear; the reporting layer was never to be named.
Separate AI agents were removed from the release after review. The system had to absorb that without starting over.

The pressure was to start with the visible AI components. I started underneath them instead, because AI patterns built on hard-coded colours and inconsistent components would have multiplied the debt.
Fixed names and states, moved colours onto tokens, replaced one-off UI-kit parts. Without this, nothing built on top could stay consistent.
Every rule in the spec became a component with variants and a written usage rule, so “what the spec says” and “what engineers build” became the same thing.
Documented it as a site people could browse, with rules, a ship checklist and descriptions engineers and AI coding tools could read.
I needed to know how far the system was from what the AI required, and how mature systems had solved the same problem.
Every component checked for hard-coded colours, naming, missing states and documentation. Result: about 8 in 10 colours hard-coded, plus a prioritised fix list.
All 23 user stories for the assistant mapped to the components they needed. Each gap became an item in the AI backlog.
How IBM Carbon for AI, SAP Fiori and Emplifi’s Soul handle AI, and where this product needed to go further.
What this product needed beyond it
A distinct visual identity for AI-generated content
Kept: a separate AI colour and badge, never used for normal actions
Kept: show sources and reasons. Added: steps that name which product the AI is using
A clear set of AI interaction patterns
Added: disclosure that scales with risk, typed confirmation, and failure states as first-class components
A principle is only useful if it ends up in something an engineer builds. I traced each one through to a rule, a component and a page of documentation.
Every change shows a plan first; risk decides how much it shows
Resolve unclear names and missing details before any plan
Each kind of failure has fixed content and never claims success
Inline notice, failed and stopped answers
Only three named tools ever appear; the reporting layer is never named
Tool steps, tools used row, details panel
Results only include what the person could see themselves
Four decisions, and what they cost
Each one had real options and a real trade-off.
The spec required confirmation inside the conversation, with no buttons. The design problem: a typed “ok” can be careless or unclear.
Buttons (ruled out by the spec); making people type an exact phrase (frustrating and error-prone); a plain question with a clear rule for what counts as yes.
Every plan ends with a specific question that names the action and the count, like “Delete these 12 items?”. I defined what counts as a yes; anything else is a no, and the AI asks again.
Slower for confident users. I kept every question short and specific, and reading data never asks for confirmation, so the extra step only appears when something changes.

k.i: The plan and question, next to the replies that do and don’t count as yes
The four plan variants side by side

k: The spec named four risk tiers but not what each should show. Without that, every feature would decide its own warnings.
A different confirmation design per feature; one design for everything; one component whose variants match the tiers.
One plan component with four variants. Reads show nothing; creates show the plan; deletes show the exact count, real names and “can’t be undone”; anything leaving the company names who is contacted.
Engineering maps each action’s tier to a variant, so a new action can’t ship without a tier, which adds a step but removes guesswork.
The AI is good at language and bad at being consistent. Some answers must be the same every time.
Let the AI decide everything; let rules decide everything and lose the natural language; split the work.
The AI understands requests and explains results. Fixed rules decide permissions, allowed status changes and risk tiers, and the design shows which is which.
Less flexible, but the same request always gets the same answer, which is what makes it trustworthy.

k.i: A status change the AI declines, with the allowed options it offers instead
Tool steps that shipped, next to the agent components kept for later

k: I had designed named agents. After review, the product team decided the assistant should stay a single AI in this release.
Throw the agent work away; push to keep it in; separate what ships now from what comes later.
Agents became tool steps like “Using workflows”, using the same trust patterns. The agent components moved to a “planned” section, documented and ready.
Two layers to maintain, but nothing was wasted and the system was ready for the next phase.
When it goes wrong, say so
Every AI gets things wrong. I treated failure as part of the system, not an edge case: each kind has a component and a fixed rule for what it must say.

Every match, with enough detail to choose

Built to be used, and kept up
A system nobody uses is useless. I treated documentation and rules for change as part of the work.
140 linked pages: foundations, every component with its real variants and properties, and the AI guidelines, clickable like a website.
Rules for every new AI feature
A ship checklist: every action needs a tier, a failure message, and only named tools, before it can ship.
Readable by people and AI tools
Clear names, a description on every component and code names on tokens, so engineers and AI coding tools build it the same way.

Design and engineering now share one definition of how the AI behaves, written down as components and rules instead of left to each feature.
What changed once engineering built with it
With ready components and written rules, engineers assembled screens instead of rebuilding parts, so new AI features came together faster.
Because behaviour and states were documented with each component, engineers had fewer questions, and handoff needed far less back-and-forth.
How often people change a plan before saying yes
Shows plans are being read and are catching mistakes
High use means the AI is often heading the wrong way
How often the AI says it can’t do something
Shows where the system and the product need to grow next
Time to design and build a new AI feature
Shows whether the system is actually speeding the team up
A design system is never finished. Testing the assistant built from it showed where the components themselves needed to change.

In testing, only 5 of 20 people checked the count before confirming a delete. The confirmation plan component will put the count and first names into the question itself, so the risk can’t be skimmed past.
18 of 20 people missed the note saying results only include spaces they can access. The note now sits above charts and tables in the answer pattern.
Add a dark set of tokens, and connect components to code so design and build stay in sync automatically.

Designing for AI means documenting behaviour, not just visuals. A design system can hold product policy, like which actions need confirmation, so designers, engineers and the AI’s own instructions follow the same rules. Fixing the foundations before adding anything new is what made that possible.

Involve engineering from the very start. Bringing engineers into the documentation from week one, instead of at handoff, would have surfaced technical limits sooner and made the components fit the build even more closely.
